stimulus.text: "I left these shores a red-hot imperialist. I wanted the American eagle to go screaming into the Pacific. … But I have thought some more, since then, and I have seen that we do not intend to free, but to subjugate the people of the Philippines. … It should, it seems to me, be our pleasure and duty to make these people free, and let them deal with their own domestic questions in their own way. And so I am an anti-imperialist. I am opposed to having the eagle put its talons on any other land." — Mark Twain, quoted in the New York World, October 15, 1900

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from Mark Twain, quoted in the New York World, October 15, 1900, public domain.
stem: Twain's position in the passage is that the United States should

options.text: Annex the Philippines to spread American ideals
options.misconception: That was Twain's old position, the one he says he held before he thought more about it.

options.text: Keep the Philippines only until Filipinos can govern themselves
options.misconception: Twain does not propose a waiting period. He says Filipinos should deal with their own questions in their own way.

options.text: Sell the Philippines to another European power
options.misconception: Twain never suggests selling the islands. His answer is freedom, not a different owner.

options.text: Leave Filipinos free to govern themselves

rationales.A: That was Twain's old position, the one he says he held before he thought more about it.
rationales.B: Twain does not propose a waiting period. He says Filipinos should deal with their own questions in their own way.
rationales.C: Twain never suggests selling the islands. His answer is freedom, not a different owner.
rationales.D: Twain's conclusion is plain: make these people free, and let them deal with their own domestic questions in their own way.
rationales.general:
1. Track the change. Twain starts as a "red-hot imperialist" and ends as an anti-imperialist.
2. Find what changed his mind. He decided America meant to subjugate Filipinos, not free them.
3. Read his conclusion. Filipinos should be free and handle their own questions in their own way.
4. Put it together. Twain's position is self-government for the Philippines, not annexation or sale.
Remember: when a writer says "I used to think," the new view is the one being argued.
